analysis.one_liner: Strips private insurers of their right to sue employers' health plans that wrongfully shift costs to Medicare.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have eliminated doubled-damages lawsuits against insurance plans that fail to pay before Medicare, was referred to two House committees and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under Medicare Secondary Payer rules, a private insurance plan must pay before Medicare when it is the primary payer, and current law lets plans and Medicare Advantage organizations sue for doubled damages when a primary plan fails to pay as required. The RAMP Act would delete that private right of action from the Social Security Act, leaving those recovery tools only to the federal government itself. The bill would have primarily shielded insurance plans from those lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers and insurance companies that run group health plans would benefit most: they could no longer be sued for double damages when they fail to make primary payment or properly reimburse, as Medicare's rules require. That removes a financial penalty for wrongfully shifting costs onto Medicare.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

how_it_helps.text: The bill's stated purpose is to repeal the private cause of action for damages against a primary plan that fails to make primary payment or appropriate reimbursement, which would spare group health plans and their insurers from doubled-damages lawsuits.

Insurers and employers argue that the private right of action generates expensive litigation and complicates settlements, particularly in liability and workers' compensation cases, and repeal would reduce that legal exposure.

analysis.who_pays: The Medicare Trust Fund and Medicare Advantage plans that rely on this right of action to recover money when a primary plan wrongfully shifts costs to Medicare; beneficiaries also lose a legal lever that holds their primary insurer accountable for actually paying first. Insurers and employers sponsoring group health plans would no longer face double-damage lawsuits when they fail to pay.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would remove the main private enforcement tool for recovering costs from primary plans that wrongfully shift them to Medicare, leaving the Medicare Trust Fund with less recourse and beneficiaries with less leverage to make sure their primary insurance pays first.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the tradeoff: the private right of action was created by law precisely because plans were not always paying appropriately, and removing it relies entirely on government enforcement to catch those failures.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow to a narrow set of insurance plans and employers that would be freed from doubled-damages liability, while the costs land on Medicare's trust fund and on Medicare Advantage plans trying to recover wrongfully shifted payments. Any savings from reduced litigation would be uncertain and largely private, while the loss of an enforcement tool is concrete. On balance, the costs to the public outweigh the private savings.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and a health subcommittee and sat there with no further action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 14, 2022, and referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee.
It was also referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was recorded after that referral.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor in its roughly six and a half months of existence, and it received no floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers, who keep the existing doubled-damages tool that pushes primary insurance plans to pay before Medicare and compensates the Medicare Trust Fund when they don't. Insurers and employer health plans, who would have gained from the repeal, did not.

industries.industry: Employer group health plan sponsors and their insurers
industries.note: The bill repeals the doubled-damages private right of action that Medicare Advantage plans and the Medicare program use to recover when a primary plan fails to pay first. Removing it lets primary plans keep more of the money they would otherwise owe, with the cost ultimately spread to Medicare and its beneficiaries.

Medicare Advantage plans are the main users of this private right of action to claw back payments from primary plans that should have paid first. Repealing it would remove their strongest recovery tool and could push costs onto premiums and taxpayers.
